stem: India is the __________ most populous country in the world.
solution: India is now the WORLD's MOST POPULOUS country, having OVERTAKEN CHINA (India's population has crossed 1.4 billion). India, with about a sixth of humanity, is one of the two demographic giants of the world (the other being China). Its huge population is a central feature of its geography, economy, and development challenges. So India is the most populous country. This is a prelims-relevant fact.

stem: The distribution of population in India is __________.
options: Uneven — some states/regions are densely populated (like the northern plains and Kerala) while others are sparsely populated (like deserts, mountains, and forests)
solution: The distribution of POPULATION in INDIA is UNEVEN. Some states and regions are DENSELY POPULATED — especially the fertile NORTHERN PLAINS (Uttar Pradesh, Bihar, West Bengal — India's most populous states) and states like KERALA and parts of the coasts and deltas — while OTHERS are SPARSELY populated — the DESERTS (Rajasthan's Thar), the high MOUNTAINS (Himalayas), and dense FORESTS and rugged areas (parts of the North-East and central India). Favourable conditions (fertile land, water, industry) attract population, while harsh terrain repels it. So India's population is unevenly distributed. So option 1 is correct.

stem: The most populous state in India is __________.
solution: UTTAR PRADESH is the MOST POPULOUS state in India — it has the largest population of any Indian state (well over 200 million people), located in the fertile Ganga plain. (Bihar, Maharashtra, and West Bengal are also among the most populous.) In contrast, SIKKIM has the smallest population among the states, and GOA and the North-Eastern states (like Mizoram) also have small populations. So the most populous state is Uttar Pradesh. This is a prelims-relevant fact.

stem: 'Population density' in India (persons per square kilometre) is highest in states/areas like __________ and lowest in __________.
options: Bihar, West Bengal, Kerala, and the NCT of Delhi (highest); Arunachal Pradesh and desert/mountain areas (lowest)
solution: POPULATION DENSITY (persons per square kilometre) in India is HIGHEST in states/areas with fertile land, good economic opportunities, or high urbanisation — such as BIHAR, WEST BENGAL, KERALA, Uttar Pradesh, and especially the NCT of DELHI (very high density). It is LOWEST in states with harsh terrain and sparse settlement — such as ARUNACHAL PRADESH and other North-Eastern hill states, and the DESERT/MOUNTAIN areas. Density thus reflects the same physical and human factors that shape distribution. So the highest densities are in Bihar/Bengal/Kerala/Delhi, the lowest in Arunachal and desert/mountain areas. So option 1 is correct.

stem: India's population has grown rapidly, and the phase of very rapid growth (the 'population explosion') occurred especially after __________.
options: 1921 (called the 'year of the Great Divide', after which population grew steadily and rapidly)
solution: India's population has grown rapidly, and the phase of very rapid growth (the 'POPULATION EXPLOSION') occurred especially AFTER 1921. The year 1921 is called the 'YEAR of the GREAT DIVIDE' in India's demographic history: BEFORE 1921, the population grew slowly and fluctuated (with periods of decline due to famines and epidemics); AFTER 1921, the death rate began to fall (due to better health, food, and control of famines/epidemics) while the birth rate remained high, so the population grew STEADILY and RAPIDLY, decade after decade. So the rapid growth began after 1921. This is a prelims-relevant fact.

stem: The main reason for India's rapid population growth in the 20th century was __________.
options: A sharp fall in the death rate (due to better health care, food supply, and control of famines and epidemics), while the birth rate remained high
A rise in the death rate
A fall in the birth rate only
solution: The main REASON for India's RAPID POPULATION GROWTH in the 20th century was a SHARP FALL in the DEATH RATE — brought about by better HEALTH CARE (medicines, vaccines, control of epidemics like plague, cholera, malaria), improved FOOD SUPPLY (agricultural advances reducing famines), and better sanitation — WHILE the BIRTH RATE REMAINED HIGH (traditional attitudes favouring large families changed only slowly). With many more people surviving but births still high, the population grew explosively. (In recent decades, the birth rate has also fallen, slowing growth.) So the cause was falling death rates while birth rates stayed high. So option 1 is correct.

stem: In recent decades, India's population growth RATE has __________.
options: Begun to slow down (decline), as the birth rate has fallen, though the total population is still increasing
Reversed into decline of total population
solution: In RECENT DECADES, India's population GROWTH RATE has BEGUN to SLOW DOWN (decline) — the RATE of increase is falling — because the BIRTH RATE has been FALLING (due to development, education, urbanisation, family planning, and changing lifestyles), moving India through the later stages of the demographic transition. Importantly, this means the TOTAL POPULATION is STILL INCREASING (as births still exceed deaths, and due to population momentum from the large young population), but at a SLOWER rate than before. So the growth rate is slowing, though the total population still rises. So option 1 is correct.

stem: 'Population composition' in India includes aspects such as __________.
options: Rural-urban composition, age structure, sex ratio, literacy, occupational structure, and linguistic/religious composition
Only the total number of people
solution: POPULATION COMPOSITION in INDIA includes several aspects: the RURAL-URBAN composition (India is still largely rural but rapidly urbanising); the AGE STRUCTURE (India has a large young/working-age population — a potential demographic dividend); the SEX RATIO (females per 1,000 males — historically adverse in India); LITERACY (which has risen but with gaps); the OCCUPATIONAL structure (a large share still in agriculture, but shifting); and the LINGUISTIC and RELIGIOUS composition (India's great diversity of languages and religions). These attributes describe the character of India's population beyond mere numbers. So India's population composition includes rural-urban, age, sex ratio, literacy, occupation, and linguistic/religious aspects. So option 1 is correct.

stem: The sex ratio in India (females per 1,000 males) has historically been __________.
options: Adverse/unfavourable to females (fewer females than males), reflecting gender discrimination, though there is some improvement over time
solution: The SEX RATIO in INDIA (the number of FEMALES per 1,000 MALES) has historically been ADVERSE/UNFAVOURABLE to FEMALES — that is, there are FEWER FEMALES than males (the sex ratio is below 1,000). This reflects deep-rooted GENDER DISCRIMINATION — son preference, neglect of the girl child, sex-selective practices, and higher female mortality in some age groups. It is a serious social concern (the 'missing women' problem). There has been SOME IMPROVEMENT over recent decades, but the ratio remains a matter of worry, especially the low CHILD sex ratio. So India's sex ratio has been adverse to females, with some improvement. So option 1 is correct.

stem: India's age structure shows that a large proportion of its population is __________.
options: Young and of working age — giving India a 'demographic dividend' opportunity (a large potential workforce)
solution: India's AGE STRUCTURE shows that a LARGE PROPORTION of its population is YOUNG and of WORKING AGE (a large share is in the 15–59/64 productive age group, and a big youth population). This gives India a 'DEMOGRAPHIC DIVIDEND' OPPORTUNITY — a large potential WORKFORCE that, IF healthy, educated, skilled, and productively employed, can drive rapid economic growth. This youthful age structure (a legacy of past high birth rates) is a major asset, but realising the dividend requires heavy investment in education, health, skills, and job creation. So India has a young, working-age population offering a demographic dividend. So option 1 is correct.

stem: The majority of India's population still lives in __________, though urbanisation is increasing.
solution: The MAJORITY of India's population still lives in RURAL AREAS (VILLAGES) — India remains a predominantly rural country, with a large share of its people engaged in or dependent on agriculture and rural livelihoods. However, URBANISATION is INCREASING rapidly: the urban population and the number and size of cities are growing steadily (through rural-to-urban migration and city growth), and the urban share is rising over time. So while most Indians are still rural, the country is urbanising. So the majority live in rural areas, though urbanisation is rising. So option 1 is correct.

stem: Assertion (A): India faces the challenge of a large and growing population. Reason (R): A large population puts pressure on resources, food, jobs, services, and the environment, requiring careful planning and development. Which is correct?
options: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A
A is true but R is false
A is false but R is true
solution: Both the Assertion and the Reason are true, and the Reason correctly explains the Assertion. It is true (A) that India FACES the CHALLENGE of a LARGE and GROWING POPULATION. And the reason is (R) that a large population puts PRESSURE on RESOURCES (land, water, energy), FOOD supply, JOBS/employment, public SERVICES (education, health, housing, sanitation), and the ENVIRONMENT — requiring CAREFUL PLANNING and DEVELOPMENT to provide for everyone and ensure sustainability. Because so many people must be fed, employed, housed, and served (and the environment protected), managing the population is a major developmental challenge (A). (A large young population is also a potential asset if well utilised.) So R correctly explains A.

stem: Literacy in India has __________.
options: Increased significantly over the decades, though gaps remain (e.g., between males and females, and between states/regions)
solution: LITERACY in INDIA has INCREASED SIGNIFICANTLY over the decades — the literacy rate has risen substantially since independence (from very low levels to a majority of the population now being literate), reflecting the expansion of education. However, important GAPS REMAIN: between MALES and FEMALES (female literacy still lags male literacy), between different STATES/REGIONS (e.g., Kerala has very high literacy, while some northern states lag), and between rural and urban areas. Raising literacy — especially female literacy — remains an important development goal. So literacy has risen significantly, but gaps remain. So option 1 is correct.

stem: The occupational structure of India shows that __________.
options: A large share of the workforce is still engaged in the primary sector (agriculture), though the shares of industry and services are growing
The service sector employs almost no one
solution: The OCCUPATIONAL STRUCTURE of India shows that a LARGE SHARE of the workforce is STILL ENGAGED in the PRIMARY sector — mainly AGRICULTURE (farming and allied activities) — reflecting India's still largely agrarian and developing character. However, the shares of the SECONDARY (INDUSTRY) and especially the TERTIARY (SERVICES) sectors are GROWING as the economy develops and diversifies (with services, including IT, expanding notably). The gradual shift of workers out of agriculture toward industry and services is a sign of India's economic development. So a large share is still in agriculture, but industry and services are growing. So option 1 is correct.

stem: India's population, being highly diverse, includes __________.
options: Many languages, religions, ethnic groups, and cultures — making it one of the most diverse populations in the world
solution: India's POPULATION is highly DIVERSE, including MANY LANGUAGES (hundreds of languages and dialects, with 22 scheduled languages), MANY RELIGIONS (Hinduism, Islam, Christianity, Sikhism, Buddhism, Jainism, and others), numerous ETHNIC groups and tribes, and a vast array of CULTURES, customs, and traditions. This makes India one of the MOST DIVERSE populations/societies in the WORLD. Managing and celebrating this diversity ('unity in diversity') is a central feature of India's demography, society, and polity. So India's population is highly diverse in language, religion, ethnicity, and culture. So option 1 is correct.

stem: India's census is conducted every __________ years.
solution: India's CENSUS — the official count of the population — is conducted every TEN YEARS (once a DECADE, a 'decennial' census). The census provides comprehensive data on population size, distribution, density, growth, and composition (age, sex, literacy, religion, occupation, etc.), which is essential for planning and administration. India's census is one of the largest such exercises in the world. So the census is conducted every ten years. This is a prelims-relevant fact.

stem: The state with the highest literacy rate in India is generally __________.
solution: KERALA generally has the HIGHEST LITERACY RATE among Indian states — it is close to universal literacy, and also has the highest female literacy. Kerala's achievements in education (and health) are often cited as a model of human development achieved through social investment despite modest income. (In contrast, some states like Bihar have had among the lowest literacy rates.) So the state with the highest literacy is Kerala. This is a prelims-relevant fact.

stem: Assertion (A): The northern plains of India are densely populated. Reason (R): The plains have fertile alluvial soil, abundant water, flat land, and a favourable climate, supporting intensive agriculture and dense settlement. Which is correct?
options: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A
A is true but R is false
A is false but R is true
solution: Both the Assertion and the Reason are true, and the Reason correctly explains the Assertion. It is true (A) that the NORTHERN PLAINS of India (the Indo-Gangetic plains) are DENSELY POPULATED — indeed, they contain India's most populous states. And the reason is (R) that the plains have FERTILE ALLUVIAL SOIL, ABUNDANT WATER (from the great rivers like the Ganga and its tributaries), FLAT LAND (easy for farming, building, and transport), and a FAVOURABLE CLIMATE — all of which support INTENSIVE AGRICULTURE and DENSE SETTLEMENT. These highly favourable conditions for livelihood and living directly explain the dense population of the plains (A). So R correctly explains A.

stem: The government's efforts to manage population growth in India have included __________.
options: Family planning/welfare programmes, promotion of small families, education (especially of women), and improving health care
solution: The GOVERNMENT's efforts to MANAGE POPULATION GROWTH in India have included: FAMILY PLANNING/family WELFARE programmes (promoting contraception and birth spacing); the PROMOTION of SMALL FAMILIES (through awareness and incentives); EDUCATION — especially of WOMEN (female education strongly lowers fertility); and IMPROVING HEALTH CARE (including maternal and child health, which, by reducing infant mortality, encourages smaller families). India launched one of the world's earliest official family-planning programmes. These measures, along with development and rising female literacy, have contributed to the falling birth rate. So India's efforts include family planning, small-family promotion, female education, and health care. So option 1 is correct.

stem: The concept of the 'demographic dividend' is especially relevant to India because __________.
options: India has a large and growing working-age population, which, if productively employed, can accelerate economic growth
solution: The concept of the 'DEMOGRAPHIC DIVIDEND' is especially relevant to INDIA because India has a LARGE and GROWING WORKING-AGE POPULATION (a youthful population, with a big and rising share in the productive age group) at a time when many other countries are ageing. If this large workforce is HEALTHY, EDUCATED, SKILLED, and PRODUCTIVELY EMPLOYED, it can ACCELERATE India's ECONOMIC GROWTH (through higher output, savings, and investment) — giving India a valuable 'dividend'. Seizing this opportunity (through investment in human capital and job creation) is a key priority; failing to do so could turn the youth bulge into a liability. So the demographic dividend is relevant because India has a large working-age population that can boost growth. So option 1 is correct.

stem: The states of the Indo-Gangetic plain (like UP, Bihar, and West Bengal) are among the __________ in India.
solution: The states of the INDO-GANGETIC PLAIN — such as UTTAR PRADESH, BIHAR, and WEST BENGAL — are among the MOST POPULOUS and DENSELY POPULATED in India. The fertile, well-watered plains have supported dense agricultural populations for millennia, and these states today contain a very large share of India's total population. (Uttar Pradesh is the most populous state; Bihar and West Bengal are also among the top and are very densely settled.) So the Indo-Gangetic plain states are among the most populous and dense. So option 1 is correct.

stem: In summary, India's population is best characterised as __________.
options: Huge, diverse, unevenly distributed, still growing (though more slowly), predominantly young and rural but urbanising — a central factor in the country's development and planning
solution: In summary, India's POPULATION is best characterised as: HUGE (the world's largest); DIVERSE (in language, religion, ethnicity, and culture); UNEVENLY DISTRIBUTED (dense in the plains and some states, sparse in deserts, mountains, and forests); STILL GROWING (though more SLOWLY now, as birth rates fall); predominantly YOUNG (a demographic dividend opportunity) and still largely RURAL but rapidly URBANISING. All of this makes population a CENTRAL FACTOR in the country's DEVELOPMENT and PLANNING — a source of both great challenges (resources, jobs, services) and great potential (a vast workforce and market). So India's population is huge, diverse, uneven, growing, young, and urbanising — central to its development. So option 1 is correct.

stem: The overall message of the chapter 'Population: Distribution, Density, Growth and Composition' (India) is that:
options: India's population is small and evenly distributed

India is the world's MOST POPULOUS country, with a large and (until recently rapidly) growing population that is very UNEVENLY DISTRIBUTED — densely settled in the fertile northern plains and states like Kerala, and sparse in deserts, mountains, and forests — with density and distribution shaped by physical and human factors; population growth was slow before 1921 (the 'Great Divide'), then rapid (a 'population explosion') due to falling death rates with high birth rates, but the growth rate has begun to slow in recent decades as birth rates fall; and India's population COMPOSITION features a largely rural but rapidly urbanising society, a young/working-age age structure (a demographic dividend opportunity), an adverse sex ratio, rising but uneven literacy, a workforce still largely in agriculture, and enormous linguistic, religious, and cultural diversity — making population a central factor in India's development
solution: The chapter's overall message is that INDIA is the world's MOST POPULOUS country, with a LARGE and (until recently rapidly) GROWING population that is very UNEVENLY DISTRIBUTED across the country. Population is DENSELY concentrated in the fertile NORTHERN PLAINS (the most populous states — Uttar Pradesh, Bihar, West Bengal — and high-density states like Kerala and Delhi) and SPARSE in the DESERTS, high MOUNTAINS, and dense FORESTS. Both DISTRIBUTION and DENSITY are shaped by PHYSICAL factors (relief, climate, water, soil) and HUMAN factors (agriculture, industry, urbanisation, transport). In terms of GROWTH, India's population grew SLOWLY and fluctuated BEFORE 1921 (the 'YEAR of the GREAT DIVIDE'), then grew RAPIDLY (a 'POPULATION EXPLOSION') from 1921 onward — mainly because DEATH RATES FELL sharply (better health, food, and control of famines/epidemics) while BIRTH RATES REMAINED HIGH — but in RECENT DECADES the growth RATE has begun to SLOW as birth rates fall (though the total population still rises). India's population COMPOSITION features: a still largely RURAL but rapidly URBANISING society; a YOUNG, working-age AGE STRUCTURE offering a DEMOGRAPHIC DIVIDEND opportunity; an ADVERSE SEX RATIO (fewer females, reflecting gender discrimination); RISING but UNEVEN LITERACY (with male–female and regional gaps); an OCCUPATIONAL structure still dominated by AGRICULTURE but with growing industry and services; and ENORMOUS LINGUISTIC, RELIGIOUS, ethnic, and cultural DIVERSITY. All this makes population a central factor in India's development, presenting both challenges (pressure on resources and services) and opportunities (a vast workforce). So the overall message is option 2.
